title: First Rust-specific package-hallucination study exists (arXiv 2606.08444): headline 22.23%, but the metric counts std items and local types; our re-extraction gives 6.1% of use-roots, 285 names, 272 currently unregistered
summary: Zheng, Guan, Liu, "When LLMs Invent Rust Crates" (Internetware 2026; arXiv 2606.08444 v2; artifacts figshare 10.6084/m9.figshare.32233767, CC BY 4.0, 154 MB): 13-14 models (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 4 Opus, Qwen2.5-Coder 0.5-32B, DeepSeek-Coder-V2 16B/236B, OpenCoder), 2,794 tasks, 16,764 snippets, 48,494 crate references, 10,779 flagged: crate hallucination rate (CHR) 22.23% overall (Gemini 16.18% to Claude 4 Opus 26.90%); 5,647 unique names after excluding module confusion; 45.47% of hallucinations are std modules misused as crates; weighted mean edit distance to nearest real crate 3.42; self-refinement cuts CHR by 2.2-3.3 points, RAG by -0.3 to 1.9. I reproduced the 10,779 / 48,494 from the artifact (rq1-a), and the top "hallucinated" entries are duration, u32, tokenstream, thread, ordering, tcplistener, atomicbool, bufreader: types and primitives, not installable names. Own re-extraction (regex for `use <root>::` and `extern crate`, excluding std/core/alloc/crate/self/super, locally declared mods and types) over 16,752 samples (3 prompt sets x 6 models): 10,462 roots, 640 (6.1%) absent from the paper's 270,227-name crates.io snapshot, 285 unique; per 999 LLM-generated prompts only 7 (Claude 4 Opus), 8 (DeepSeek, GPT-5), 12 (Gemini, Qwen), 30 (OpenCoder) samples (0.7% to 3.0%) contain a missing root. Live sparse-index check 2026-10-25 (no registration performed): 13 of the 285 now exist (abi, ark_bls12_381, assert_eq, inline_string, interface, mediapipe, my_macro, oncelock, thread_count, tok, ts_types, winhttp, x86_64), 272 are absent (many are placeholders such as crate1/foo_v2/another_crate, Windows import libs such as kernel32/gdi32, rust-analyzer internals ide_db/hir, or vendor-prefix guesses such as apache_arrow, aws_sdk_core, alloy_rpc). Refutes r1 sc.slopsquat-rates "no crates.io-specific measurement exists".
overclaim_risk: My regex ignores grouped use trees, fully-qualified paths and Cargo.toml dependencies; generated code contains many example placeholders; the paper's snapshot date is not stated; the model set (Claude 4 Opus, GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Qwen2.5-Coder) predates 2026 frontier models, and no agent loop with cargo add was tested.
underclaim_risk: Even at 0.7-3% of samples, a single registrable name that recurs across models (the Spracklen result: 43% of names repeat across 10 reruns) is exploitable; 272 names are claimable today and an agent running `cargo add` for a missing root would hit it. The 6.1% of use-roots dwarfs the zero measured crates.io slopsquat incidents, so exposure is real but unrealized.
specifics: Extends sc.slopsquat-rates (reuse id). L5 acceptance metric: seed 500 server-coding prompts, count roots not in the live crates.io index; track per model release; threshold: any root resolving to a crate younger than 90 days or with <100k recent downloads blocks `cargo add` in the agent sandbox. Artifact inspected locally then deleted (halluc_summary.json, halluc_live.json kept).

verify.note: Paper verified (22.23%, 10,779/48,494); paper says 16,764 snippets vs explorer 16,752; re-extraction not reproducible by verifier.

title: Incident to gate back-test (12 incidents 2024-2026): vet+new-name+14-day cooldown stops 10/12; SLSA L3 verify + TUF alone stop 2/12; TUF stops 0/12
summary: Each incident coded for whether a gate applied at dependency intake would have stopped the malicious artifact reaching a build (2 stops, 1 partial/conditional, 0 no, NA). Incidents: xz-utils 5.6.0/5.6.1 (2024-02-24 to 03-29, 34 d), ultralytics 8.3.41-46 (2024-12), tj-actions/changed-files CVE-2025-30066 (2025-03-14, tags moved, 3 d), faster_log/async_println (2025-05-25 to 09-24, 122 d), evm-units/uniswap-utils (2025-04 to 12-02, ~230 d), Nx s1ngularity (2025-08-26, 4 h), chalk/debug +16 (2025-09-08, ~2.5 h), Shai-Hulud wave 1 (2025-09-14..23), Shai-Hulud 2.0 (2025-11-21..24; PostHog 5 h 19 m publish-to-removal), Polymarket typosquats tracings (2026-02-26, ~9 h), Trivy v0.69.4 / TeamPCP CVE-2026-33634 (2026-03-19..22), arrayref 0.3.10 / internment / append-only-vec (2026-08-20, 86-107 min). Stops (of applicable): cargo-vet 4/5 (Rust-only; partial xz), new-name/age gate 3/4, cooldown 7 d 6/12 (+3 partial), 14 d 8/12, 35 d 8/12 (+2), trusted-publishing+attestation-required 2/12 (+7 partial), SLSA L3 provenance verify 2/12 (+3), reproducible independent rebuild 4/12 (+3), tarball-vs-git 3/10, SHA pinning 2/2 applicable, TUF 0/12. Combination vet+new-name+14 d cooldown 10/12 (misses xz and tj-actions-by-mutable-tag); adding SHA-pin, reproducible rebuild and tarball parity 12/12. The window medians matter: 8 of 12 had a public exposure window under 7 days (Yossarian 2025-11-21 found 8 of 10 under a week in a different incident set), the long-dwell cases are the typosquats and xz.
overclaim_risk: Cell values are my counterfactual judgments (not executed against the real artifacts); selection is the incidents named in the brief plus the 2026 additions (not a random sample); npm/PyPI incidents are mapped to a hypothetical Rust consumer; exposure windows come from secondary reports for chalk, Nx and Shai-Hulud; n=12 so single flips move fractions by 8 points.
underclaim_risk: Even as judgment, the ordering is robust: gates that act on time and novelty (cooldown, vet on new crates) dominate gates that act on provenance, and no single gate covers more than 8/12 (14 d cooldown, 35 d cooldown).
specifics: Raw matrix in 04-work/matrix.json. Contrarian conclusion: SLSA L3 provenance is necessary for our OWN release (it stops the build-host class for us) but as a consumer-side control on 2024-26 dependency incidents it stops 2/12 outright, because 9/12 were produced by legitimate pipelines or legitimate credentials. Extends sc.slsa-attest (grade B, build-host claim) and sc.cooldown-policy; closes q1-077.

verify.note: Self-scored counterfactuals over 12 hand-picked incidents; post-hoc gate stacking; arrayref credential cause inferred.

title: Of 12 incidents 2024-26: 5 CI/build-pipeline (42%), 3 maintainer credential or machine (25%), 3 new malicious packages (25%), 1 social-engineered insider (8%); 3 of 5 CI cases name pull_request_target
summary: Classification: CI/build pipeline: ultralytics (GitHub Actions cache poisoning, then leftover PyPI token), tj-actions (reviewdog/spotbugs pull_request_target PAT chain, tags moved), Nx (pull_request_target PR-title injection, npm token), Shai-Hulud 2.0 via PostHog (2025-09-11 pull_request_target change, static-analysis alert dismissed, malicious PR 2025-11-18 ran <1 min and stole bot PAT, malicious publish 2025-11-24 04:11 UTC, removed 09:30 UTC), Trivy/TeamPCP (misconfigured workflow let a bot leak a privileged PAT, non-atomic credential rotation on 2026-03-01, malicious release 2026-03-19, backdoor injected at release build so Homebrew source builds were unaffected). Maintainer credential/machine: chalk/debug (npmjs.help TOTP phishing 2025-09-08), Shai-Hulud wave 1 (token theft and worm republish; CISA 2025-09-23 >500 packages, initial access not stated), arrayref/internment/append-only-vec (Rust blog 2026-08-20: maintainer computer or credentials likely compromised; new account impersonating dtolnay published typosquat proc-macro1 first). New malicious packages: faster_log/async_println, evm-units/uniswap-utils, Polymarket typosquats. Insider: xz (first contribution 2021-10-29, org member 2022-10-28, releases 2024-02-24/03-09, disclosure 2024-03-29). So the build-host/CI-secret class (42%) is the largest and its root cause in 3 of 5 (Nx, PostHog, tj-actions chain) is an explicit pull_request_target workflow, in the others a workflow injection/cache or credential-rotation failure.
overclaim_risk: n=12 and selection by prominence; classes overlap (Shai-Hulud 2.0 is both CI-initiated and token-propagated; arrayref root cause is not published); Nx and chalk root causes come from vendor write-ups.
underclaim_risk: The CI-workflow class is bigger than the credential class and is entirely preventable by a 5-minute linter gate plus a rule that findings cannot be dismissed without a CODEOWNER; that gate is missing from most supply-chain checklists that stop at SBOM/provenance.
specifics: Excluded from the denominators: crates.io GitHub-login phishing 2025-09-12 (Rust blog; no malicious publish stated) and rustdecimal (2022-05). Extends sc.gha-hardening and rec60-supply-chain-incidents; closes q1-077 fraction question.

verify.note: n=12 non-random; Trivy arguably credential as much as CI; PostHog timeline verified.

title: SLSA v1.2 states what Build L3 does not cover: malicious producers, dependencies, social/review attacks, and anything the consumer does not verify; Trivy and ultralytics show the legitimate pipeline producing the malicious artifact
summary: slsa.dev/spec/v1.2/threats: malicious producer "cannot be directly mitigated through SLSA controls"; dependency threats "not explicitly addressed"; collusion, bugdoors and rubber-stamped reviews "not currently addressed"; protection applies "when the consumer verifies artifacts against expectations"; Source track L2+ blocks history rewrite and tag replacement, L4 requires approval of every change. Incident fit: ultralytics round 1 was published by Trusted Publishing from the legitimate workflow (cache poisoned), round 2 by a leftover API token with no attestation (provenance policy catches only round 2); Trivy v0.69.4 was built by the official release pipeline from a poisoned workflow commit (provenance would be valid; an independent source rebuild, e.g. Homebrew, was clean); PostHog 2.0 malicious versions came from a direct push of a workflow change by a stolen bot PAT. Consumer-side L3 verify would have stopped chalk-style hand-published versions and arrayref (no attestation) only if the project previously published with attestations.
overclaim_risk: Spec text and two incident write-ups; I did not retrieve in-toto attestations for Trivy.
underclaim_risk: The same SLSA text supports using provenance for our own releases: it removes artifact-substitution and token-misuse, the class that is 42% of incidents when combined with reproducible rebuilds.
specifics: Extends sc.slsa-attest. Practical rule: provenance is evidence, an independent rebuild is a test; require both (B/L5 gate sc3.l5-release-attest-rebuild).

verify.note: Spec scope well grounded; Trivy official-pipeline detail not confirmed (Wiz says stolen release credentials).

title: rustls 0.23.46 (2026-10-14) fixed four advisories incl. unauthenticated ServerHello downgrade to classical key exchange; rustls-webpki 0.103.16 (2026-10-20) fixed distrusted-intermediate acceptance
summary: RUSTSEC-2026-0346 (Debug impls expose TLS secrets), -0347 (buffered data to outer server after ECH rejection), -0348 (brotli certificate decompression allocates up to 1 GiB before authentication), -0349 (unauthenticated ServerHello can downgrade later connections to classical key exchange) all dated 2026-10-14, patched >= 0.23.46; RUSTSEC-2026-0382 / CVE-2026-111943 (2026-10-20) emSign intermediates; tokio 1.54.0 UAF RUSTSEC-2026-0384 (fixed 1.54.1, 2026-10-21) and RUSTSEC-2026-0386 (patched >=1.51.6<1.52, >=1.53.3). The golden pin rustls >=0.23.46 is therefore a security floor, not a preference; rustls-webpki >=0.103.16 and tokio >=1.54.1 should be floors too.
overclaim_risk: Titles and dates read from advisory-db files; I did not test exploitability.
underclaim_risk: These land within the window where any 7-14 day cooldown would have held production on vulnerable versions; they are the executed evidence for a security-bypass clause.
specifics: L5: Cargo.toml floors rustls = ">=0.23.46", rustls-webpki = ">=0.103.16", tokio = ">=1.54.1" plus cargo-deny [advisories] so a downgrade by cooldown fails CI. Extends crate-rustls-pq and rec60-supply-chain-incidents.

title: L5 CI gate list for the golden: 9 gates with exact commands, thresholds and the executed numbers that set them
summary: G1 lock-intake: `cargo deny --locked check advisories bans licenses sources` (deny.toml: yanked=deny, unmaintained=all, multiple-versions=deny with skip = the 6 measured duplicates only, wildcards=deny, 11-SPDX allowlist) AND `cargo audit --deny warnings` (advisory-db commit age < 24 h) AND `cargo vet --locked` (six imports; exemptions count may only decrease; baseline unaudited 116 on linux tree; any NEW crate must be audited or imported, never exempted). G2 cooldown+bypass: see sc3.l5-cooldown-security-bypass. G3 reproducible double build: sc3.l5-repro-double-build. G4 tarball-vs-git parity: sc3.tarball-git-parity-golden (0 unexplained diffs; allowlist aws-lc-sys:aws-lc/**, ring:pregenerated/**). G5 new-crate intake: sc3.l5-new-crate-intake. G6 CI workflow lint: sc3.l5-workflow-lint. G7 unsafe ceiling: `cargo geiger --all-targets=false --output-format Json` vs unsafe-allowlist.json (sc3.geiger-014-golden-unsafe seeds); first-party `unsafe_code = "forbid"` in [workspace.lints.rust]. G8 release attest+rebuild: sc3.l5-release-attest-rebuild. G9 embedded SBOM: `cargo auditable build --release --locked` then `cargo audit bin <artifact> --deny warnings` (executed: 190 deps embedded, 0 vulns; hash differs from non-auditable build, so reproducibility compare is done on the shipped mode). Gate order is cheapest-first: G6 (seconds), G1, G5, G4, G7, G3, G8, G9.
overclaim_risk: Gates are only as good as the allowlists; vet imports measure other people's reviews.
underclaim_risk: All thresholds are anchored to executed numbers on the pins, so they are testable rather than aspirational.
specifics: Acceptance criterion: a clean checkout of the golden commit passes G1-G9 in CI with zero manual overrides; each gate has a negative control (a PR that adds a typosquat dependency, a pull_request_target workflow, an extra unsafe block, a tarball-modified vendored file, a path-dependent build) that must fail. Maps to ops.ssdf-12-ci-gates (PS.2.1, PS.3.2, PW.6, RV.1-3) and ops.cra-obligation-split (SBOM+provenance steward file set).

verify.note: Composite design; end-to-end G1-G9 pass never shown; G8 infra absent.

title: L5: dependency cooldown of 7 days with an auditable security-advisory bypass (not 14 days, not unconditional)
summary: Policy: .cargo/config.toml [registry] global-min-publish-age = "7 days" once the pinned toolchain is >= 1.100 (on 1.99.x use the nightly flag only in an update bot, never in the release build; release builds use --locked and are unaffected). Updates happen only through a bot PR created by `cargo update` under the cooldown. CI job after every lock change: (1) `cargo audit --deny warnings`: if it names an advisory whose patched version is newer than the cooldown, the PR must carry the label `security-advisory` and the commit message `CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_PUBLISH_AGE=allow cargo update -p <crate> --precise <patched>`; (2) script queries crates.io created_at for every changed lock entry and fails if age < 7 days and the label is absent; (3) override needs a vet delta audit or a trusted-publisher entry plus second human approval, expiry 30 days. Why 7 and not 14: executed 7-day resolution produced 1 advisory (webpki), 14-day produced 6 (rustls x4, webpki, tokio) and a hard resolver failure on an exact pin; windows for 8 of 10 public attacks were under 7 days (Yossarian), 6 of 12 stopped at 7 d vs 8 of 12 at 14 d in our matrix, the 2 extra stops (Trivy images, Shai-Hulud wave 1) are long-tail. Exact first-party pins (=) are incompatible with cooldown; use caret ranges plus the lock.
overclaim_risk: Cooldown protects only against fast-detected compromises; xz (34 d) and the crates.io typosquats (122-230 d) pass it; the 7 d vs 14 d trade is inferred from n=12.
underclaim_risk: Dependabot now defaults to a 3-day wait and security updates bypass it; cargo 1.100 makes this native and preserves the override in the lockfile.
specifics: Extends sc.cooldown-policy and v.cargo-min-publish-age-rfc3923; closes q1-052 (exact cargo version: cargo 1.98.0 has -Z only; stable in 1.100.0; RFC 3923 merged 2026-05-18).

title: L5: reproducible double-build gate with exact flags, pass criterion and negative control
summary: Pinned toolchain via rust-toolchain.toml channel = "1.99.1" (digest of the channel manifest recorded in the attestation). Job builds twice in different working dirs with different CARGO_HOME and SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH: `export RUSTFLAGS="--remap-path-prefix=$PWD=/src --remap-path-prefix=$CARGO_HOME/registry/src=/cargo/registry --remap-path-prefix=$RUSTUP_HOME=/rustup"; cargo fetch --locked; cargo build --release --locked` with [profile.release] lto=true codegen-units=1 panic=abort (debug 0 or 2). Pass: sha256sum(binA)==sha256sum(binB). Negative control (must FAIL): the same build without the registry remap (measured: differing 242 path strings, sizes differ 704 bytes). Weekly: a second runner on a different OS image rebuilds from the git tag and compares to the published hash (cross-host spike not yet done). Build mode must equal the shipped mode (cargo auditable changes the hash). Do not ship from a build whose hash was not reproduced.
overclaim_risk: Same-host proof only; aws-lc-sys C compilation depends on the system compiler version.
underclaim_risk: Costs about 2 minutes per build on 4 cores for a 233-crate lock.
specifics: Extends sc.repro-build-experiment; closes q1-092 on 1.98.0/1.93.1 here and 1.99.1 per R199 field of sc3.repro-ablation-golden; q1-041 (cross-machine, StageX) remains an implementation-phase spike: protocol = build in two distro images (debian:13 vs ubuntu 26.04) with identical toolchain tarball, compare sha256, diff with diffoscope.

title: L5: new-crate intake gate for agent-added dependencies (slopsquat and typosquat), thresholds calibrated on 2025-26 cases
summary: Trigger: any Cargo.lock diff that adds a crate name. Script (crates.io API, 1 req/s): fail unless (a) the crate is covered by an imported cargo-vet audit or first-party audit, or (b) age of first version >= 90 days AND recent_downloads >= 100,000 AND owner set unchanged for 90 days; always fail if Damerau-Levenshtein distance <= 2 to a top-1000 crate by downloads and the name is not in an allowlist, or if the crate has a build.rs/proc-macro and age < 365 days. Calibration: faster_log (7,181 dl, 122 d) and evm-units (7,257 dl, ~230 d) pass an age-only gate but fail the 100k download gate and vet; proc-macro1 (arrayref, hours old, impersonating dtolnay) and the Polymarket crates (9 h) fail the age gate; the paper reports mean edit distance 3.42 to the nearest valid crate for hallucinated names, so an edit-distance <=2 rule alone will miss most slopsquats and the download/age/vet rules must carry the load. Agent sandbox: `cargo add` wrapper that runs this gate and has no write token for crates.io.
overclaim_risk: Thresholds (90 d, 100k, 365 d) are my choices from 5 cases; popular crates with real small maintainers fail it and need a human.
underclaim_risk: The vet rule alone stopped all 3 new-malicious-crate incidents plus arrayref's new dependency (4 of the 5 Rust-applicable cases); the gate list is deliberately redundant.
specifics: Extends sc.crates-malicious-record (its thresholds were E-graded) and sc.slopsquat-rates; closes q1-028.

title: L5: CI workflow lint that cannot be dismissed (zizmor + CODEOWNERS + SHA pins), aimed at the 42% CI-class incidents
summary: Commands: `zizmor --pedantic --min-severity low .github/workflows` must exit 0; grep gate: every `uses:` pinned to a 40-hex SHA; top-level `permissions: {}`; forbid `pull_request_target` combined with `actions/checkout` of `github.event.pull_request.head.*`; no `${{ github.event.* }}` interpolated into `run:` (PR title/branch injection as in Nx); caches are not shared between untrusted PR workflows and release workflows (ultralytics); release job uses a protected GitHub environment with required reviewer, trusted publishing only, and long-lived publish tokens deleted (ultralytics round 2). Suppressions: `# zizmor: ignore` lines and any dismissal require a CODEOWNER review of .github/ (PostHog dismissed the static-analysis alert on the 2025-09-11 change that was used for the 2025-11-18 attack). Credential rotation after any incident must be atomic (Trivy 2026-03-01 rotation was not).
overclaim_risk: Static lint cannot see a compromised runner image or a stolen human credential.
underclaim_risk: It addresses the largest class (5 of 12) with a seconds-long job; in 3 of those 5 the vulnerable construct is a one-line trigger.
specifics: Extends sc.gha-hardening (same tool, now tied to incident counts).

title: L5: release gate = provenance + independent rebuild + branch protection (SLSA Build L3 and Source L2), not provenance alone
summary: Release workflow (reusable, signing in a separate job): actions/attest@v4 with id-token: write, attestations: write; verification in a clean container: `gh attestation verify ./srv -R <org>/<repo> --signer-workflow <org>/<repo>/.github/workflows/attest.yml`. Add: (1) independent rebuild on a second runner image from the signed tag, hash must equal the attested subject digest (this is what detected Trivy v0.69.4 in the wild: source builds by Homebrew were clean); (2) protected default branch with required reviews and no force-push/tag replacement (SLSA Source L2+, the control that prevents the tj-actions retroactive tag move); (3) crates.io trusted publishing only for our own crates with token publishing disabled; (4) consumers' policy: reject versions whose trustpub/attestation disappears for a crate that had it. Pass: verify exit 0 AND rebuild hash equal AND tag object signed.
overclaim_risk: Still trusts GitHub runners and Sigstore; fails to a legitimately merged malicious commit (xz-class).
underclaim_risk: Provenance plus rebuild covers 6 of 12 incidents in the matrix versus 2 of 12 for provenance alone.
specifics: Extends sc.slsa-attest and sc.sigstore-tuf-threshold. TUF (0/12) belongs to the update channel for the deployed server (rollback/freeze protection), not to dependency intake.

title: arrayref 0.3.10: the compromised-publisher case defeats cargo-vet publisher trust but not new-crate vet; cooldown of 1 day would have stopped it (86-107 min live)
summary: RUSTSEC-2026-0260: arrayref 0.3.10 published 2026-08-20, live ~86 min, 2,285 downloads (<10% of its traffic); append-only-vec 0.1.9 published 07:37:49Z deleted 09:25:24Z (107 min); the malicious versions added a dependency on proc-macro1 (typosquat of proc-macro2 created that morning by a new account impersonating dtolnay) whose build script ran the payload; arrayref was republished with the newest versions yanked to force resolution. Vet: trusted-publisher entries (mozilla 262, bytecode-alliance 165 in r1) would auto-accept a version from a compromised trusted account, but the new dependency proc-macro1 was unaudited so `cargo vet --locked` fails; lockfile consumers were largely unaffected (RUSTSEC text: "most users were on older versions pinned in their lockfiles").
overclaim_risk: Attribution claims (DPRK overlap) come from a single AI-assisted CSA note and are unverified; I do not use them.
underclaim_risk: Shows --locked as the first line of defense and cooldown as the second; also that `cargo vet trust` expands the blast radius to everything the publisher owns.
specifics: Extends sc.arrayref-incident. L5 consequence: do not use `cargo vet trust` for crates reached by build scripts or proc-macros; require per-version audits there.

title: draft-niyikiza-oauth-attenuating-agent-tokens-01 (Attenuating Agent Tokens), 2026-06-15
summary: Individual I-D (OAuth header, Standards Track intent, not WG-adopted), expires 2026-12-17. Offline-derivable JWT chain: child signed by parent's cnf key, par_hash = SHA-256 of parent JWS signing input, invariants I1-I6, RAR authorization_details mapping tool -> argument constraints. Authorization uses the LEAF token's constraints only, so safety rests on a correct subsumption checker (I4).
specifics: Rev -00 (Mar 2026), -01 2026-06-15. Ed25519 MUST; alg allowlist, reject none. Claims jti, iss (JWK thumbprint URI of parent holder key), iat, exp, cnf, del_depth, del_max_depth, par_hash; no sub. Constraint types exact, range, one_of, not_one_of, contains, subset, wildcard, all, any; unknown type -> deny; closed-world maps must keep same keys. PoP = custom JWT (not DPoP RFC 9449) carrying aat_id, aat_tool, OPTIONAL aat_aud, hta = JCS(args); +/-30 s window; stateless PoP must not be used for side-effecting calls (needs jti store, backend undefined). MAX_IAT_SKEW 30 s; MAX_TOKEN_LIFETIME <= 90 days; MAX_TOKEN_SIZE 64 KiB; MAX_CONSTRAINT_DEPTH 32. Revocation (s8.9) out of scope: short TTL + root rotation. CWT/COSE profile deferred (App. D) though the reference impl (Tenuo) uses CBOR/COSE. Alloy model: no counterexample up to 8 constraints x 8 values (bounded, not a proof). No PQ alg named; cnf.jwk not hardcoded so RFC 9964 AKP keys are possible.
overclaim_risk: It is an individual draft by the vendor of its reference implementation; no WG adoption; 'Standards Track' is the intent only.
underclaim_risk: Its I1-I6 invariant list and par_hash anti-splicing binding are directly reusable in our wire format whatever we choose.

verify.note: -01 2026-06-15 exp 2026-12-17 confirmed; author also wrote reference impl.

title: draft-asor-wimse-agent-delegation-chain-02 (Verifiable Attenuated Delegation for AI Agent Chains), 2026-10-15
summary: Individual I-D (WIMSE header), sole author R. Asor (Attenu), expires 2027-04-18. JWT (at+jwt) delegation tokens with mandatory JCS, mandatory aud, sub invariance, par_hash, DPoP holder binding, Token Status List revocation (unknown status denies), and cumulative constraints. Argues RFC 8693 nested act is audit-only per RFC 8693 s4.1.
specifics: Revisions -00, -01, -02 (2026-10-15). Algs: Ed25519 REQUIRED, ES256 OPTIONAL, ML-DSA (RFC 9964) OPTIONAL; verifier takes alg from its own key config and denies a mismatch even if the signature verifies (algorithm-confusion defense). JCS rejects duplicate members, non-finite numbers, lone surrogates, ints > 2^53-1. del_depth == position; del_max_depth non-increasing; exp non-increasing; only DT_n aud checked. Verification: sigs -> par_hash (constant time) -> depth/principal -> subsumption -> time -> DPoP -> status list -> aud + authorize incl. cumulative constraints (running total from a separate channel). Denial names: signature_invalid, par_hash_mismatch, not_narrower.
overclaim_risk: One-author individual draft; WIMSE has not adopted it.
underclaim_risk: It is the only agent-chain draft found that combines mandatory aud, DPoP, revocation and an ML-DSA alg; it is the closest standards candidate for our cross-domain Tier X wire format.

verify.note: -02 2026-10-15 exp 2027-04-18 confirmed with Ed25519 MUST, ML-DSA optional, mandatory aud, unknown status denies.

title: RFC 9964: ML-DSA for JOSE and COSE (Prorock, Steele, 2026, Proposed Standard)
summary: Registers ML-DSA-44/65/87 for JOSE ('ML-DSA-44' etc.) and COSE (-48/-49/-50), new key type AKP (COSE kty 7), seed-only 32-byte private keys. This gives any JWT/CWT capability chain a standard PQ algorithm id.
specifics: Sizes (FIPS 204): ML-DSA-44 pk 1312 / sig 2420 B; ML-DSA-65 pk 1952 / sig 3309 B; ML-DSA-87 pk 2592 / sig 4627 B. JWS base64url adds ~33%: one ML-DSA-65 hop (sig + inline cnf pk) ~ 7.0 KB encoded, already near nginx's 8 KB default single-header buffer; a 3-hop chain cannot travel in one header.
overclaim_risk: RFC existence does not mean JOSE libraries ship it: jsonwebtoken 11.1 only mentions ML-DSA in jwk.rs; biscuit, rs-ucan, tenuo-core, superfly/macaroon, cedar have no PQ code (grep 2026-10-25).

title: Microbench: per-token verify cost, Biscuit vs HMAC-chain vs opaque handle vs signature floors (measured 2026-10-25)
summary: Single thread on one laptop. Biscuit 6.0.0 full parse+verify+authorize: 64.7 us for 1 block (213 B), 158 us for 3 blocks (466 B). Signature verification is about 90% of that (143 us for 3 blocks). A 5-caveat HMAC-SHA256 chain verifies in 1.23 us (112 B). An opaque 256-bit handle with SHA-256 and a 1e6-entry HashMap lookup takes 83 ns. ML-DSA-65 verify is 114 us vs Ed25519's 33 us, so a PQ Biscuit-style per-block-signature design costs at least about 114 us per block.
specifics: i9-14900HX laptop, 1 thread, nice 15, cgroup MemoryMax 6G, rustc 1.98.0 --release, 5 trials median, 2026-10-25. Crates: biscuit-auth =6.0.0, hmac =0.12.1, sha2 =0.10.9, fips204 =0.5.0, ed25519-dalek 2.2.0. Results (median ns/op): biscuit 1 blk 64,655; 3 blk 157,983; 3 blk parse+sig only 143,208; hmac chain 1 caveat 423, 5 caveats 1,229; opaque handle 83; ed25519 verify 32,925; ML-DSA-65 verify 113,918; ML-DSA-44 verify 69,122. Ratios: Biscuit-3 / HMAC-5 = 129x; Biscuit-3 / handle = 1,900x. Projected PQ Biscuit (ML-DSA-65 per block, 3 blocks) >= 3 x 114 us + Datalog ~15 us ~= 360 us and ~16 KB raw. Bench source: scratchpad tokbench/src/main.rs (re-creatable from the spike protocol).
overclaim_risk: Microbenchmark, not system throughput; ed25519-dalek at 33 us is slower than typical published figures (~15-25 us) because of nice 15, CPU scaling and no explicit SIMD backend, so absolute numbers are pessimistic. The ratios are the finding.
underclaim_risk: Even 158 us is fine for many APIs. The cost matters at agent-swarm request rates and on a $5 VPS (1 vCPU: ~6k Biscuit verifies/s vs ~800k HMAC verifies/s).

verify.note: One laptop CPU at nice 15; ratios robust to 2x error.

title: Biscuit default RunLimits max_time = 1 ms wall clock: an authorize() returned Err(RunLimit(Timeout)) locally on a trivial token
summary: Across 3 runs: run 0 panicked on a single RunLimit(Timeout); a contended run (load average ~60-70 from sibling builds) produced 5 Timeout denials in 40,800 authorize() calls on trivially valid tokens (0.012%), with 0 when max_time = 1 s; a quiet run produced 0/40,800. The check is Instant::now() >= start + max_time inside run_with_limits (datalog/mod.rs:619-663), so decisions depend on scheduler load. It fails closed (deny), so it is a liveness and determinism defect, not a bypass. It breaks deterministic-replay and DST oracles.
specifics: RunLimits::default() = {max_facts:1000, max_iterations:100, max_time:1ms} (6.0.0 datalog/mod.rs:750-756). Mitigation if Biscuit were used: set_limits(max_time = large) and rely on max_facts/max_iterations (deterministic) plus an outer fuel budget. Neil Madden (2022) notes Datalog's PTIME guarantee is data complexity; program complexity is exponential, and Biscuit lets token holders add rules, which is why a wall-clock guard exists at all.
overclaim_risk: Rate measured only on one loaded laptop (0.012% under heavy contention, 0% quiet); production frequency is unmeasured.
underclaim_risk: Under agent-swarm load (the exact time authz matters most), wall-clock limits turn CPU contention into authorization denials and nondeterministic audit logs.

verify.note: Artificial contention; documented 1 ms default; panic may be harness unwrap.

title: Tenuo 0.3.3 (feature 'cel'): CEL attenuation check is syntactic and strips whitespace inside string literals, so a child can widen authority. Confirmed locally; unfixed on main 2026-10-24
summary: CelConstraint::validate_attenuation (tenuo-core/src/constraints.rs:3899) accepts a child if normalize(child) starts with '(' + normalize(parent) + ')&&' and the remainder has balanced outer parens. normalize = split_whitespace().join("") also removes spaces inside string literals, and the paren check ignores literals. Chain verification (planes.rs verify_chain_link) reuses this check and authorization evaluates only the LEAF (planes.rs:1426 leaf.authorize), so an accepted child is real amplification.
specifics: Local test against v0.3.3 (cel feature): (a) parent `value == "a b"`, child `(value == "ab") && (true)`: validate_attenuation = Ok; parent.matches("ab") = false, child.matches("ab") = true. (b) child `(value == "a b") && ("(") || true || (")")`: validate_attenuation = Ok; child.matches("zzz") = true (CEL || absorbs the && type error), so the child is unconstrained. Default features exclude cel, so default builds are unaffected. Tenuo's own SECURITY.md rates 'Monotonicity violation' as High. DISCLOSURE: report privately to security@tenuo.ai before any public use of these details; this repo must not publish the PoC strings.
overclaim_risk: Affects only deployments that enable 'cel' and accept CEL constraints from token holders. Not a signature forgery.
underclaim_risk: It is an existence proof of the general hazard: any design where the verifier checks a subsumption relation and then evaluates only the leaf inherits every bug in the subsumption checker. Macaroon/Biscuit-style 'evaluate every caveat in the chain' is immune by construction.

verify.note: SECURITY.md confirmed (High, security@tenuo.ai); PoC not re-run; non-default feature, 2k downloads.

title: Attacker-on-each-candidate matrix: confused deputy, replay, audience confusion, attenuation bypass, clock skew
summary: Each candidate attacked from spec text and code. The opaque handle and the HMAC chain with key-separated audience and required exp have the fewest open cells. Biscuit's weak cells are its rule/check interplay (needs correct origin scoping, unproven) and the lack of built-in PoP. AAT/Tenuo depends on a subsumption checker (bug confirmed). TE+act has unenforced depth >= 2 and splicing. ZCAP had a depth-2 expiry bug.
specifics: Confused deputy: bearer formats (Biscuit, macaroon, JWT) need PoP (DPoP RFC 9449 / cnf caveat) or a sender-bound handle; UCAN and ZCAP have signed invocations built in; AAT has a custom PoP. Replay: all need jti/nonce state for side effects (AAT says so explicitly); the handle can be single-use atomically. Audience: plain macaroons have none unless the root key is per audience (derive K_aud = HKDF(K, aud)); Biscuit has none unless a check is added (no mandatory field); AAT aat_aud OPTIONAL; DT aud REQUIRED (leaf only). Attenuation bypass: Biscuit, if a block or authorizer uses trusting previous / a 3rd-party key (CVE-2024-41949 class) or authority rules derive from authorizer facts; AAT/Tenuo via the subsumption checker (r3e05.tenuo-cel-attenuation-bypass); TE via splicing and informational act; ZCAP via the per-depth expiry check (CVE-2024-31995); JWT libs via type confusion (CVE-2026-25537). Clock skew: AAT 30 s iat skew + 30 s PoP window; Biscuit time is an authorizer-supplied fact (the authorizer controls the clock, plus the wall-clock run limit); same-host issuer=verifier (handle, Tier L) needs no skew allowance.

verify.note: Qualitative and partly circular; cells map to cited advisories.

title: Token decision for the golden: Tier 0 opaque handle + server-side capability table (default); Tier L macaroon-style HMAC-SHA256 chain in verified deterministic CBOR for offline holder attenuation; Tier X COSE_Sign1 ML-DSA-65 (RFC 9964) root only at trust-domain crossings. External OAuth/AAT/DT tokens are accepted only at ingress and exchanged into Tier 0/L. Biscuit, UCAN and ZCAP are rejected for the golden.
summary: This descends l5-authz-stack-recommendation with a code-level instrument and makes the r1 'own two-tier format' concrete: (1) the issuer and the verifier are the same server in the golden, so asymmetric offline verification buys nothing there. (2) Cost: handle 83 ns, HMAC-5 1.2 us, Biscuit-3 158 us, PQ per signed block >= 114 us. (3) Every caveat in the chain is evaluated (conjunction), so monotonicity holds by construction and does not depend on a subsumption checker (Tenuo bug). (4) The parse surface is a verified CBOR parser. (5) Revocation is instant via the table or a nonce row. Cedar 4.14 stays the PDP: token caveats become Cedar context/entities, and Cedar decides.
specifics: Pins: cborrs vendored from everparse tag v2026.10.07 (sha256 of the tree recorded in vendor/README); hmac =0.12.1 + sha2 =0.10.9 (or aws-lc-rs HMAC in FIPS mode); fips204 0.5.0 or aws-lc-rs ML-DSA for Tier X; cedar-policy =4.14.0. Rejected: Biscuit (no PQ enum, 15-month-old release, wall-clock limits, holder-supplied Datalog = exponential program complexity, 129x the HMAC verify cost; reversal below); UCAN (no released 1.0 Rust crate, no PQ); ZCAP (JSON-LD canonicalization surface, JS ecosystem, CVE-2024-31995); TE+act as internal authority (informational act, AS round-trip per hop); AAT/Tenuo as internal format (leaf-only evaluation needs a subsumption proof; no revocation). REVERSAL CONDITIONS: (R1) a golden deployment needs third parties to verify our tokens offline without a shared secret: promote Tier X to the full chain format, and prefer draft-asor DT if it gains a CWT profile; (R2) the AAT or DT draft is adopted by OAuth/WIMSE with a COSE profile and ML-DSA: adopt it as the Tier X wire format; (R3) Biscuit ships a PQ algorithm + deterministic fuel limits + a formal scoping model: reconsider it for Tier X; (R4) Tier 0 table lookup with ancestor walk exceeds p99 5 us at depth 8 or the table cannot be replicated for multi-node: move the default to Tier L; (R5) Cedar lands a delegation RFC (watch rfcs PR stream; #114 is attestation only).
overclaim_risk: The golden's issuer=verifier assumption is a design choice. Multi-node deployments need the table replicated or the HMAC key shared (KMS/HKDF), which adds a key-distribution TCB.
underclaim_risk: Rejecting Biscuit forgoes its rich Datalog caveats; our closed caveat set must cover real agent needs (tool, argument constraints, resource prefix, op mask, tenant, exp, aud, cnf), or users will smuggle logic into Cedar context.

verify.note: Issuer=verifier premise single-server only; EverParse dir lists cbordet*.rs, crate name unconfirmed; RFC 9964 and asor-02 confirmed.

title: Tier L wire format + Lean-ready invariants: deterministic-CBOR HMAC chain with closed caveat set, required aud/exp, cnf binding
summary: The wire format is a CBOR array of version, kid, nonce, caveats and tag. Caveats come from a closed tagged set. The denotation is the conjunction of every caveat, and the tag is an HMAC chain keyed from K_aud = HKDF(K_master, 'aegis-cap-v1' || aud || kid). The Lean statements are given so that monotonicity, audience binding, expiry and depth bounds are theorems over a pure model. The Rust verifier is then DRT-checked against the Lean executable model.
specifics:
CDDL: token = [1, kid: bstr .size 8, nonce: bstr .size 16, caveats: [1*64 caveat], tag: bstr .size 32]; caveat = [1, aud: tstr .size (1..253)] / [2, exp: uint] / [3, nbf: uint] / [4, ops: uint] (bitmask) / [5, res_prefix: tstr] (canonical path, no '..', NFC) / [6, cnf_jkt: bstr .size 32] / [7, tenant: bstr .size 16] / [8, tool: tstr, argc: {* tstr => argcon}] / [9, depth_left: uint .le 8]; argcon is exact / range / one_of only (no regex, no CEL). Deterministic encoding per RFC 8949 s4.2.1; any non-canonical or unknown tag is rejected at parse (cborrs). Max encoded size 4 KiB. MAC: t0 = HMAC(K_aud, kid||nonce); t_i = HMAC(t_{i-1}, enc(caveat_i)); tag = t_n; compare in constant time. Mint rules: >=1 aud caveat equal to the minting audience, exactly one exp at mint with exp - now <= MAX_TTL (default 900 s), depth_left present.
Lean 4 (core only, no Mathlib): structure Req := (aud : String) (op : Nat) (res : String) (tenant : ByteArray) (holder : ByteArray) (tool : String) (args : ...) (now : Nat). def sat : Caveat -> Req -> Bool. def denote (cs : List Caveat) (r : Req) : Bool := cs.all (sat . r). Theorems: (T1 attenuation_mono) forall cs c r, denote (cs ++ [c]) r = true -> denote cs r = true. (T2 aud_bound) wellMinted cs -> denote cs r = true -> r.aud = mintAud cs. (T3 expiry) wellMinted cs -> denote cs r = true -> r.now < mintExp cs, and appended exp caveats only lower the effective expiry: effExp (cs ++ [exp e]) = min (effExp cs) e. (T4 depth) appending is allowed only if depth_left > 0, and the effective depth_left is non-increasing. (T5 verify_iff) verify K t r = true <-> (macChain K t = t.tag /\ denote t.caveats r), with HMAC as an opaque function (EUF-CMA is an explicit assumption, not proven). (T6 parse_canonical) taken from cborrs (EverParse proof) and cited, not re-proven. Clock: issuer and verifier share a host clock, so the skew allowance is 0 for exp and nbf. Multi-node: <= 2 s skew bound, stated as an assumption.
overclaim_risk: T5 proves the model, not the Rust; Rust refinement rests on DRT plus optional Verus. HMAC security is assumed.
underclaim_risk: T1-T4 are near one-line proofs (List.all_append), cheap enough that no proof-synthesis LLM is needed (§0c).

verify.note: Unchecked theorem statements; HMAC opaque; skew figures assumed.

title: Verifier fuzz-harness spec for the Tier L/0 token verifier (cargo-fuzz + DRT + mutation gate)
summary: Nine targets with acceptance criteria. They cover the bug classes found in this round's advisory and code survey: signature forgery, type-confused exp/nbf, depth-specific expiry skip, subsumption-checker amplification, third-party key confusion, wall-clock nondeterminism and parser differentials.
specifics: F1 parse_canonical: arbitrary bytes -> parse; if Ok then serialize(parse(b)) == b (round-trip) else reject; zero panics. F2 bitflip_reject: valid token + 1 random bit flip/insert/delete -> verify = false (except in unused padding; there is none). F3 mono_prop: arbitrary (token, caveat, req) -> verify(append(t,c), r) implies verify(t, r). F4 drt_lean: generate (t, r) from a structured Arbitrary -> Rust verify == Lean-compiled denote/verify executable (with HMAC replaced by a deterministic test PRF on both sides), 0 divergences over 1e8 cases per release. F5 type_confusion: exp/nbf/aud encoded with the wrong CBOR major type, negative ints, floats, bignums, duplicate map keys, indefinite lengths -> reject (JWTFuzz-inspired). F6 depth_matrix: every caveat type at chain positions 0..8 -> identical semantics at every depth (zcap CVE-2024-31995 class). F7 audience_keysep: a token minted for aud A presented to B -> reject; also kid rollover. F8 time_boundary: now in {exp-1, exp, exp+1} and {nbf-1, nbf} -> exact outcomes; the verifier takes now as a parameter (no ambient clock) so DST is deterministic. F9 resource_bounds: 64 caveats / 4 KiB max -> verify time O(n) with p99 <= 5 us for 8 caveats on the 2-vCPU reference VPS, and no allocation > 8 KiB. CI gates: 1e8 execs per target per release with 0 crashes; cargo-mutants kill rate >= 90% on verifier.rs; F4 0 divergences; F9 perf regression <= 10%. Also run the same F2/F5/F7 corpus against any Tier X and ingress JWT verifier (jsonwebtoken >= 10.3.0 pinned; required_spec_claims = [exp, aud]).

verify.note: Spec only; thresholds arbitrary; F4 DRT hard.

domain: W-BRIDGE (W-STATE x W-DATA-GATE x W-TRANSPORT x W-ISOLATION)
title: Async cancellation (future drop at an await) is one root cause behind pooled-connection poisoning, cross-request data leaks, leaked server-side state, host panics and lost/locked state
summary: Across 15 independent instances in 5 ecosystems (Rust sqlx, tokio-postgres, diesel_async, Wasmtime, oneshot, Oxide omicron; Python redis-py; Go database/sql and lib/pq; Node pg-pool), the same shape recurs: an operation puts a request on a wire or takes a resource BEFORE its first suspension point, but the value whose cleanup undoes it is built AFTER the last response. Dropping the future in between leaves the resource mid-protocol, and the pool or runtime then REUSES it. The resulting failure classes are: (1) the next borrower gets the previous request's response (redis-py CVE-2023-28858/28859, the ChatGPT incident of 2023-03-20; Go CVE-2025-47907; diesel_async #304); (2) the next borrower runs inside a stale transaction (sqlx #4393); (3) server-side objects are leaked (tokio-postgres PR #1374, node-postgres #3543); (4) a stray cancel hits the next query (lib/pq #1000); (5) the Wasm host panics or a component instance cannot be re-entered (CVE-2026-27195, RUSTSEC-2026-0354); (6) in-process state is left inconsistent (omicron PR #3140); (7) liveness is lost (futurelock, omicron #9259). The attacker controls the timing: hyper drops the service future on a client RST_STREAM or a closed connection.
specifics: Count of verified instances: 15 (10 Rust, 5 non-Rust). In 2026 alone there were 6 (sqlx #4393 on 2026-08-24, tokio-postgres #1374 on 08-03, diesel_async #304 on 10-18, Wasmtime CVE-2026-27195 on 02-24 and RUSTSEC-2026-0354 on 10-14, oneshot RUSTSEC-2026-0005 on 01-25). Fixes for 3 of the 6 are on main but UNRELEASED as of 2026-10-25: sqlx (latest release 0.9.0 is from 2026-05-21; the fix f1e94ec is 2026-09-09), diesel_async (latest v0.9.2 is from 2026-06-19; PR #305 merged 2026-10-23), tokio-postgres (PR #1374 is still open; latest 0.7.18). Hypothesis verdict: SUPPORTED for the DB-pool, Wasm-host and in-process classes. It is NOT the root cause of the 'idempotency key stored without result' class (crash/timeout without cancellation produces the same failure, so cancellation is one trigger among several). For fail-open on timeout it is only partial: that is a policy choice, as in the Bitwarden code.
overclaim_risk: 'One root cause' overstates it. Idempotency rows stuck in_flight and INCR/EXPIRE TTL loss happen equally from crashes, and fail-open-on-timeout is a deliberate policy (Bitwarden). Cancellation is the most frequent trigger in async Rust, but crash and timeout share the remedy.
underclaim_risk: Counts are lower bounds. Searches covered only issue titles and bodies with 'cancel' wording, and many such bugs get filed as 'wrong result' or 'connection reset' without naming cancellation.

verify.note: Core URLs resolve except rust-lang/rust-postgres (repo is sfackler/rust-postgres); sqlx moved to transact-rs; 'one root cause' fits DB-pool subset, Go/oneshot/futurelock mechanistically different.

title: hyper 1.12 drops the in-flight service future on h2 RST_STREAM (H2Stream::poll2 -> poll_reset) and on h1 connection close: a remote client picks the cancellation instant
summary: Read from the hyper main source (src/proto/h2/server.rs): while the service future is Pending, H2Stream polls reply.poll_reset(cx). On a reset it returns Err('stream received RST_STREAM'), and the service future is dropped at whatever await it is parked on. h1 does the same through Dispatcher drop of in_flight. An unauthenticated client can measure handler latency and send RST_STREAM (or a FIN) to land the cancellation between, for example, COMMIT-sent and outcome-recorded, or between INCR and EXPIRE. tower-http 0.7.1 Timeout polls its Sleep before the inner future, returns 408, and drops the inner future even if it already committed.
specifics: Cancellation sources as listed by Oxide RFD 400: select!, timeout, try_join, task abort, runtime shutdown. Plus the server-specific ones: h2 RST_STREAM, h3 STOP_SENDING/RESET_STREAM, h1 close, tower timeout, graceful-shutdown deadline, Wasm epoch trap. Dual failure: when cancellation is NOT propagated (Pingora RUSTSEC-2025-0070 / CVE-2025-8671 MadeYouReset), handler work keeps running after the reset and causes a resource DoS. Go net/http TimeoutHandler returns 503 while the handler goroutine continues, so a failure is reported to the client while the effect still happens. The server must handle BOTH directions.
overclaim_risk: Precise timing over the internet is noisy. An attacker needs many attempts, but rapid-reset-style volume is cheap.
underclaim_risk: Agents that retry with aggressive timeouts (MCP clients, LLM tool loops) trigger the same cancellations without any malice, so this is a correctness issue at agent-era retry rates, not only an attack.

verify.note: hyper poll_reset and tower-http Timeout verified in source; RUSTSEC-2025-0070 is pingora-core not hyper; future-drop after reset inferred.

title: sqlx #4393: cancelling Pool::begin leaves the PG connection inside a transaction and poisons the pool; fix #4394 (f1e94ec, 2026-09-09) is on main but not in any release
summary: PgTransactionManager::begin raised transaction_depth only after the BEGIN round trip, so a cancelled begin queued no ROLLBACK. return_to_pool's ping() drains ReadyForQuery but ignores the transaction-status byte. The next borrower then runs inside the stale transaction (holding its locks) or hits 25P02 on every query until max_lifetime. This is the 4th cancel-safety fix to BEGIN in four years: #2054 (2022-08), #2819 (2023-10), #3980 (2025-08), #4394 (2026-09).
specifics: State left: open txn on a pooled conn, locks held, possible 'idle in transaction (aborted)'. Fix state: merged to main 2026-09-09; sqlx 0.9.0 (2026-05-21) is still the latest release, and main is 41 commits ahead of v0.9.0. Downstream forks backport it (lexe-app to 0.8.6). sqlx 0.9.0 pool docs: if acquire() is cancelled after obtaining a conn, the conn is DROPPED (deliberately not graceful), and for PG/MySQL that drop closes only the client side, so the server may keep running until TCP keepalive. Clauses violated: INV-NOMUT (a stale txn could be committed by the next borrower; in this BEGIN case there were no writes, but the lock holding is observed), CRS C8 (shared-context partitioning: one connection carries two principals' txn context), C6.
overclaim_risk: The cancellation window is the BEGIN round trip only, so it needs a timeout or disconnect during BEGIN. It is narrow, but an attacker can target it.
underclaim_risk: If the golden uses sqlx 0.9.0 from crates.io it ships with this bug. Pin to git rev f1e94ec or later, or wrap acquisition in our own guard.

verify.note: Issue/PR/merge sha f1e94ec 2026-09-09 verified; 41 commits ahead of v0.9.0; '4th fix' count partly unsupported.

title: tokio-postgres PR #1374 (open, 2026-08-03): a dropped prepare()/bind()/savepoint future strands named statements, portals and savepoints for the session; it fires on plain timeout(d, client.query(..))
summary: Written by the deadpool maintainer. Parse/Bind/SAVEPOINT go on the wire before the first yield, but Statement/Portal/Transaction (whose Drop sends Close or ROLLBACK TO) are built only after the last response. The fix adds a DropGuard armed right after send and disarmed when the owner takes over. That is safe because Close of an unknown name is not an error, and Close travels FIFO on the same channel. For savepoint, the guard disarms on failure because RELEASE of a missing savepoint would poison the transaction.
specifics: tokio-postgres 0.7.18 (2026-06-12) is affected. The PR has 4 commits, including failing tests in tests/test/cancellation.rs; co-authored with Claude Opus 5 per the commit trailer. Companion: #1394 (2026-10-20, open): prepare() returns Ok while a trailing ErrorResponse 57014 (statement_timeout) is dropped. The txn is aborted and the next statement fails with 25P02, which is the same 'reply not drained to ReadyForQuery' root. Clause: resource budgets I1 (server-side memory grows per cancelled request, so an attacker can grow PG backend memory with RST floods) and CRS C8.
overclaim_risk: It leaks memory, not data. Prepared statements are per-session and invisible to other principals.
underclaim_risk: On a long-lived pooled connection, the leak accumulates until max_lifetime, and an attacker controls the rate.

verify.note: Real at sfackler/rust-postgres PR #1374 (open 2026-08-03) and #1394 (2026-10-20); cited URLs 404.

title: diesel_async #304 (2026-10-18): MySQL query future dropped -> conn back to bb8/deadpool -> the next borrower reads the cancelled query's result; fix PR #305 merged 2026-10-23, unreleased
summary: The default PoolableConnection::is_broken checked only the transaction manager, not mysql_async's Conn::is_disconnected() flag (set at the start of each command, cleared at completion, public since 0.37). The trigger is tokio::time::timeout or an axum/hyper handler dropped on client disconnect. Symptoms: 'Record not found' and parse errors, which means the previous principal's rows are delivered to the next request. The PG backend already checked is_closed(). Earlier cancel bugs in the same crate: #281/#282 (2026-03, SyncConnectionWrapper panic) and #270 (2025-11, CannotCache statement leak when a stream is dropped).
specifics: Fix state: main only; latest release v0.9.2 (2026-06-19). Clauses: CRS C8 (response queue shared between principals), confidentiality/tenant isolation, INV-NOMUT (a wrong result can drive a wrong write). This is the Rust twin of redis-py CVE-2023-28858.

verify.note: Verified; PR #305 merged 2026-10-23; symptoms incl. 'Packets out of sync'; v0.9.2 latest.

title: redis-py CVE-2023-28858/28859 (#2624, 2023-03-17): cancel after send, before read, leaves the reply on a pooled connection -> off-by-one responses to unrelated clients (OpenAI ChatGPT incident 2023-03-20)
summary: The reproducer showed get('bar') returning b'foo' and get('foo') returning b'PONG'. The first fix (4.5.3, #2641) was incomplete per the reporter, was re-tracked in #2665, and was fixed by #2695 (closed 2023-06-27). The CVE record was created in response to the ChatGPT reports.
specifics: Fixed in 4.3.6/4.4.3/4.5.3 (partial) and later in 4.5.5+/5.0. NVD rates it low (CVSS 3.7) even though it caused a production cross-user data exposure, so CVSS underrates this class. Clauses: CRS C8, tenant isolation.

verify.note: Issue names no CVE; NVD CVSS unverified; first fix was #2641 (still reproduced on 4.5.3); #2695/2023-06 unconfirmed.

title: Go CVE-2025-47907 / GO-2025-3849 (go#74831): cancelling the context during Rows.Scan with parallel queries returns another query's results; 'affects most database/sql drivers'
summary: Reported by Coder. Fixed in go1.23.12 and go1.24.6, published 2025-08-07. Even Go's preemptive goroutine model gets cross-query result leaks from context cancellation racing driver buffer reuse.
specifics: Clauses: CRS C8, confidentiality. Contrast lib/pq PR #1000 (2020-10-02, merged 2020-11-24): a ctx-timeout CancelRequest raced connection return, so the cancel hit the NEXT query on the reused connection. Fix: mark the conn bad (follow-up #1079). pgx v4+ policy (pgx#679, 2020): on ctx cancel, close the connection and send CancelRequest rather than try to recover it (discard-on-cancel).

verify.note: GO-2025-3849 and go#74831 verified; pgx#679 is an unrelated issue; lib/pq #1000 verified.

title: The Postgres CancelRequest addresses a backend (PID+key), not a statement, gets no reply, and 'might or might not have any effect'; protocol 3.2 (PG18) lengthens the key (4..256 B, server sends 32) but leaves targeting unchanged
summary: PG 18 docs 54.2.8: the frontend has no direct way to tell whether a cancel succeeded. Because the cancel races with completion, a cancel sent for query A can land on query B on the same backend after a pool reuse (lib/pq #1000, pgx#679 discussion). So 'send CancelRequest then reuse the connection' is unsafe. The only safe options are close-and-discard, or wait for ReadyForQuery after the cancel before reuse.

verify.note: Documented protocol behaviour; not re-fetched.

title: Wasmtime: 2 cancel-on-drop advisories in 8 months: CVE-2026-27195 / RUSTSEC-2026-0022 (drop call_async after guest yields -> instance non-reenterable -> host panic) and GHSA-3r89-v5mq-j5xf / RUSTSEC-2026-0354 (drop of a queued call_async -> unwrap panic in Drop)
summary: CVE-2026-27195 (2026-02-24): affects 39.0.0..<40.0.4 and 41.0.0..<41.0.4; 42+ unaffected; trigger is an async hostcall (func_wrap_async) or an EPOCH INTERRUPTION yield, then a drop. RUSTSEC-2026-0354 (2026-10-14, PR #14741): affects >=46.0.0; patched >=48.0.6,<49 and >=49.0.3. The Drop impl for the call_async future looked for the task's work items in only one of several queues. Both come from the component-model-async surface, which the map already flags as dominating 2026 Wasmtime advisories.
specifics: State left: the component instance cannot be re-entered (the guest's linear memory is mid-operation), and the host panics, which violates I5 (no panic reachable from network input). An h2 RST is network input that drops the future. Mitigation: per-request Store/instance discarded on any cancellation (never reuse a Store after a dropped call_async, as the advisory workaround also says); disable component-model-async unless needed; pin wasmtime >= 49.0.3 (or 50.0.0).

verify.note: CVE-2026-27195 (39.0.0-41.0.3, needs component-model-async) and GHSA-3r89 (no CVE, 5.9, 46-<48.0.6, 49-<49.0.3) verified; host panic needs embedder dropping call_async.

title: oneshot RUSTSEC-2026-0005 (2026-01-25): a Receiver polled and then dropped (for example by a timeout) races the Sender's free -> use-after-free; fixed in 0.1.12
summary: Cancellation reaches memory safety even in safe-API crates built on unsafe internals. Drop swapped the state to DISCONNECTED before reading its waker back. This is a reason to keep the golden's channel primitives to tokio's audited ones and to fuzz drop-after-poll under Miri/loom.

verify.note: RUSTSEC-2026-0005 informational/unsound; fixed 0.1.12; GHSA-rvr2.

title: Oxide omicron PR #3140 (2023-05): a client disconnect cancelled an endpoint holding a tokio Mutex mid-sequence -> protected data left inconsistent; led to dropshot HandlerTaskMode::Detached (#695/#701)
summary: dropshot #695: futures returned by endpoints 'may be cancelled under the control of the client'. The chosen band-aid was to tokio::spawn handlers (Detached) instead of auditing every endpoint. Dropshot 0.17.1 exposes HandlerTaskMode {CancelOnDisconnect, Detached}. Follow-ups: #965 (on_disconnect scopeguard, 2024), #1359 (500 vs 499 in detached mode, 2025), #1677 (2026-08, open: panics reported as disconnects). This is Java's Thread.stop lesson again: ThreadDeath released all monitors and left 'damaged objects', and Thread.stop was deprecated for that reason. Dropping a tokio MutexGuard at an await is the same failure confined to await points.

verify.note: dropshot#695 verified, fixed via PR #701; omicron #3140 is 'Spawn a task to run services_ensure'.

title: Futurelock (Oxide RFD 609, omicron #9259, 2025-10-19): a select! over &mut future holding a fair tokio Mutex slot plus an await in another arm hung every DB-touching request in Nexus
summary: This is not cancellation. It is the opposite failure: a future started and then never polled again while it holds a resource. Mitigations: spawn and select on the JoinHandle; JoinSet instead of FuturesUnordered when awaiting in the loop body; try_send with propagated errors. RFD 609 proposes two clippy lints (a &mut future in a select! arm; await inside a select! arm), and neither exists as of 2026-10.

verify.note: omicron#9259 exists but closed 2025-10-19; absence-of-lint claims unverified.

title: Rate-limit counter written as INCR then EXPIRE across two awaits: a crash or cancel between them leaves TTL=-1 and the identity is limited permanently (GitLab gitlab#285352, 2020; fixed by a single Lua EVAL plus self-heal in labkit-ruby 99204787)
summary: A cancel at the await between INCR and EXPIRE produces the same state as the observed crash. The inverse is just as bad: a limiter that debits AFTER the handler (post-hoc cost, I5) loses the debit when the handler future is dropped, which gives the attacker free work. Also: Bitwarden server CustomRedisProcessingStrategy (last commit fa0c9cb, 2025-07-08) returns SkipRateLimitResult (Count=0) on RedisTimeoutException, on !IsConnected, or after N timeouts. That is deliberate fail-open, and an attacker who can induce Redis latency disables IP rate limiting.
specifics: Clauses: abuse I5 (post-hoc debit lost), I7 (no-fail-open; Bitwarden violates it by design), I4. Rule: debit atomically BEFORE the work (single script or op), never refund on cancel, and charge cancellations themselves, as HAProxy glitch counters and Go too_many_early_resets do.
overclaim_risk: GitLab's root cause was a crash or ordering problem, not an observed cancellation. The cancel mapping is by mechanism, not by report.

verify.note: GitLab issue verified but crash-triggered, not cancellation; Bitwarden fail-open is policy.

title: node-postgres pg-pool #3543 (2025-09-09, open): a connectionTimeoutMillis race leaves a server-side idle connection that pg-pool tracks but never marks idle until the pool closes
summary: This is the Node analogue of sqlx's 'acquire cancelled after connect'. A timeout on the client side does not undo server-side resource creation. Oracle: pg_stat_activity rows with query_start IS NULL and state='idle'.

verify.note: Issue verified open; resource leak via timeout race, not dropped future or data exposure.

title: Timeout after commit makes the observed failure differ from the actual outcome: tower-http Timeout returns 408 and drops an inner future that may already have committed; Go TimeoutHandler returns 503 while the handler keeps writing
summary: This is the 'ambiguous commit' carve-out of sdg-failed-request-no-mutation, turned from a rare network event into a routine, timer-driven and attacker-reachable one. A client told 408/503 retries, which double-applies the effect unless an idempotency key covers it. The amendment needs a commit-point latch: after COMMIT is sent, no timer or disconnect may convert the outcome into a failure status.

verify.note: tower-http source verified; ambiguity only when drop lands between COMMIT sent and reply.

title: Cancellation models compared: Rust drop (sync cleanup only, no shield) vs Python/Trio exception-at-checkpoint (async cleanup, shield, flake8-async lints) vs Java interrupt (Thread.stop removed) vs Go context (cooperative)
summary: Python 3.15 asyncio: CancelledError is a BaseException, cleanup in finally can await, asyncio.shield exists, TaskGroup/timeout rely on cancellation, and uncancel() exists. flake8-async provides a cancellation lint family: ASYNC100 (cancel scope with no checkpoint), ASYNC101/119 (yield in a cancel scope), ASYNC102 (await in finally/except needs a shield), ASYNC120, and ASYNC910/911 (off by default). PEP 789 (Draft) proposes sys.prevent_yields. Java deprecated asynchronous Thread.stop because of damaged objects. Rust: cleanup is Drop, synchronous only, with no shielded region except tokio::spawn. AsyncDrop is a nightly experiment (rust-lang/rust#126482, open since 2024-06-14; the 2026-07-14 comment says the dyn case is unhandled) and is not on the 2026 'just add async' roadmap. Even with async drop, mem::forget and leaks mean cleanup is not guaranteed. Linear (must-complete) futures exist only as stale experiments: the completion crate 0.2.1 (2021) and moro 0.4.0 (2022).
specifics: Implication: in 2026 Rust offers no language or lint guarantee of cancel correctness. Assurance must come from architecture (spawn to completion, discard on cancel, a sans-IO core) plus dynamic testing (cancel sweep). Unique Rust strength: cancellation can only happen at await points, which are finite and enumerable per execution, unlike Thread.stop, which could hit any instruction.

verify.note: verifier sampled other nodes; explorer grade kept

title: Rust cancel-safety tooling, 2026-10: clippy has the configurable await_holding_invalid_type and disallowed_macros but no cancel-safety lint; async-rust-lsp is editor-only; no crate exists for cancel-at-every-await testing; asupersync is an unproven cancel-correct runtime
summary: clippy: await_holding_invalid_type (1.62, suspicious, configured via clippy.toml await-holding-invalid-types and able to cover tokio::sync::MutexGuard), await_holding_lock, await_holding_refcell_ref, let_underscore_future (warn by default; catches the 'async refactor drops the future' bug from RustConf 2025), disallowed_macros (1.66, style; can ban tokio::select!), disallowed_methods/types. async-rust-lsp 0.3.1 (rgbkrk, 2026-04): rules mutex-across-await (tokio) and cancel-unsafe-in-select (read_exact/write_all in a select! arm). It has no CLI, so it cannot be a CI gate as-is. cancel-safe-futures 0.1.5 (Oxide, 2026-04-01; coop_cancel, then_try). tokio-util 0.7.20 CancellationToken. asupersync 0.5.0 (2026-09-12; 287 stars; license NOASSERTION; request->drain->finalize cancellation, regions, two-phase reserve/commit effects, deterministic lab runtime): interesting design evidence, but a full runtime replacement with unknown audit status, so reject for the golden and revisit if independently audited. Five crates.io searches found no 'cancel at every await' test crate.
specifics: Oxide RFD 400 gives the vocabulary. Cancel safety is local; cancel correctness is global; a violation needs a cancel-unsafe future, its cancellation, and a broken system property. Patterns: reserve/permit split, resume from progress, avoid tokio::sync::Mutex, spawn to completion, cooperative cancel, check connection state at the START of a txn, and a '# Cancel safety' doc section. tokio 1.54.1 select! docs list the cancel-safe and unsafe methods (read_exact, read_to_end, read_to_string and write_all lose data; Mutex::lock, RwLock, Semaphore::acquire and Notify::notified lose queue position).
underclaim_risk: A dynamic 'poll N then drop' sweep is simple to build, about 100 LOC. The absence of a crate is no reason to skip it.

verify.note: verifier sampled other nodes; explorer grade kept

title: Counter-hypothesis test: 'one transaction per request + effects journaled after commit' closes about 5 of 15 instances; the residual 10 need discard-on-cancel, a commit-point latch, pre-debited accounting and no tokio Mutex
summary: CLOSED by one-txn+outbox: uncommitted partial DB writes; idempotency key without result (if the idem row shares the txn); pre-commit external effects (if handlers have no direct effect capability); cross-system effects (outbox with deterministic keys); in-txn SET LOCAL tenant settings. NOT CLOSED: (a) client-side protocol state on pooled connections (sqlx #4393, diesel_async #304, redis-py, Go 47907, lib/pq, tokio-postgres #1374, pg-pool #3543): the server rolls back, but the CONNECTION is reused mid-protocol, so you need discard-on-cancel plus a ReadyForQuery status 'I' check at checkin; (b) ambiguous outcome after COMMIT-sent (tower-http 408, Go TimeoutHandler): you need a commit-point latch; (c) in-process state under tokio Mutex (omicron #3140); (d) security accounting, which MUST mutate on failure (rate-limit debits, auth-failure counters, audit records), so blindly applying the invariant to them creates free retries (I5); (e) Wasm instance state (CVE-2026-27195, RUSTSEC-2026-0354); (f) liveness (futurelock); (g) streaming: a txn held open during a slow-read stream is an attacker-held lock (DoS), and per-chunk commits break the one-txn rule, so commit before the first body byte (output gate) or stream from a read-only snapshot with a deadline; (h) server-side work continuing after client cancel (the PG query runs until keepalive or CancelRequest), which costs resources, not consistency; (i) non-transactional backends with no rollback (Redis without MULTI, S3, Kafka without EOS) need the outbox.
specifics: Verdict: the rule is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT. The amended invariant must add a cancellation clause family (ac.l5-inv-nomut-c).
overclaim_risk: The 5/15 vs 10/15 split depends on how the instances are partitioned. Some, like Go 47907, are read-side leaks that the rule never claimed to cover.

verify.note: verifier sampled other nodes; explorer grade kept

title: Design principle: cancel == crash of the request's domain (Candea & Fox, 'Crash-Only Software', HotOS IX 2003): never recycle a resource a cancelled request touched mid-operation
summary: The DB already treats a client crash correctly: a closed connection rolls back the txn. Bugs appear when a cancelled request is treated as a soft stop and its half-used resources are recycled. So make cancellation equivalent to a crash of the request's domain: close its DB connection(s) if not provably idle, discard its Wasm Store, close its upstream connection, and drop its scratch state. Cost: connection churn that attackers can amplify (each RST potentially forces a PG reconnect). Bound it by charging cancellations to the client's budget (same accounting as Rapid Reset). pgx v4+ is a production existence proof (close + CancelRequest on every ctx cancel).
specifics: Unmeasured: PG reconnect cost. The only source found is an unsourced vendor estimate of 50-100 ms; spike: pgbench -C vs persistent at TLS+SCRAM on a 1 vCPU box. Mitigation if expensive: discard only when the connection is NOT in ReadyForQuery 'I' with no outstanding replies. That needs a driver that exposes the state, which tokio-postgres does not today, so the golden's DB adapter must track it.

verify.note: verifier sampled other nodes; explorer grade kept

title: INV-NOMUT-C: 'failed or cancelled request => no business-state mutation, fail-closed authz, monotone accounting' with clauses NC1-NC8
summary:
DEFINITIONS. Request domain D(r) = every resource r acquired: DB connections and txns, named server objects (statements, portals, savepoints), Wasm Store/instance, upstream connections, in-process guarded objects, idempotency rows, budget reservations. Commit point CP(r) = the instant the COMMIT of r's single txn (or the atomic local flush) is handed to the wire. Outcome(r) is in {Committed, Failed, Pending}. A termination is any end of r's handler future: return, error, panic, timeout, client disconnect (h1 close, h2 RST_STREAM, h3 STOP_SENDING/RESET_STREAM), task abort, runtime shutdown, Wasm trap/epoch deadline, process crash.
NC1 Cancellation is failure: every termination before CP yields Outcome=Failed, and INV-NOMUT applies (no durable user-visible business row changed, modulo sequences).
NC2 Commit-point latch: from CP on, r is non-cancellable. COMMIT, the outcome record (idempotency row = done + response) and the outbox flush run to completion in a runtime-owned task registered with the shutdown drainer, independent of the client connection. The response status derives only from the commit result. A timer or disconnect after CP may yield only 'Pending' (202 + retrieve by idempotency key), never 408/5xx implying failure.
NC3 Discard-on-cancel: any resource in D(r) that was mid-operation at a termination is never reused. Pool checkin predicate reusable(c) := last frame was ReadyForQuery AND txn_status=='I' AND outstanding_replies==0 AND every server object r created is closed. Otherwise close it (optionally send CancelRequest first, but never reuse after a CancelRequest). A Wasm Store whose call_async future was dropped is discarded. Upstream HTTP connections with unread response bytes are closed.
NC4 Monotone accounting: security-accounting state (rate/budget debits, auth-failure counters, audit-of-attempt records) is written BEFORE the work it meters, as a single atomic op (no read-modify-write and no INCR-then-EXPIRE across an await). It is never refunded on failure or cancel, and every cancellation is itself charged (cost >= 1 unit). It is EXEMPT from NC1.
NC5 Fail-closed on cancel or timeout: a cancelled, timed-out or panicked authz/limiter/verifier stage evaluates to Error, and Error => Deny (vfg tri-state). No 'skip limiting on backend timeout' path exists in the golden.
NC6 No effect before CP: handler code holds no capability for external effects. Effects are outbox rows inside the txn, dispatched after CP with keys derived deterministically from (tenant, idempotency key, effect index).
NC7 Output gate for streams: response body bytes that depend on uncommitted writes are emitted only after CP. No txn stays open while waiting on client reads or writes (a slow reader must not hold locks). Streams read from a committed snapshot or a read-only txn with a deadline <= T_stream_max.
NC8 Liveness: no started future that holds a shared resource is left unpolled (futurelock). Every in-flight handler finishes or is discarded within T_drain after termination, and resources return to the pool or are closed within that bound.
specifics: Clause cross-map: NC1/NC2 refine sdg-failed-request-no-mutation INV-NOMUT (they turn the 'ambiguous commit' carve-out into a latch). NC3 extends CRS C8 (shared-context partitioning: a reused connection mid-protocol IS a response queue shared across principals) and C6 (failure atomicity: a cancelled validation is a failed validation). NC4 refines abuse I5 (debit before work, not post-hoc, because post-hoc debits are lost on drop) and I4. NC5 is the cancellation case of vfg-policy-tristate-failclosed-invariant and abuse I7. NC6 is sdg-exactly-once-boundary. NC8 extends I1 (bounded resources per request). INV-NONEMPTY is untouched but depends on NC3: a leaked txn carries the previous request's SET LOCAL role/tenant into the next borrower, so NC3 is a precondition for tenant binding. Survivability against arbitrary third-party modules: NC1, NC3, NC4, NC5 and NC8 are enforced by the host (it owns the pool, the Store, the limiter and the drainer), so they SURVIVE a malicious sandboxed module. NC2, NC6 and NC7 hold only for DB access mediated by the golden SDK and Ctx; an out-of-process adapter with its own pool must re-prove NC3 (a conformance-suite case). Proof plan: NC2/NC3 as a TLA+ or P model of the request state machine {Admitted, Running, CommitSent, Committed, Failed, Discarded} with cancellation as a nondeterministic action enabled in Running only; NC4/NC5 as GCRA/tri-state lemmas (Kani/Lean, reusing existing obligations); all clauses tested by ac.l5-cancel-sweep-harness.
overclaim_risk: NC2 makes the commit non-cancellable, so a slow COMMIT (sync replication wait) delays shutdown. This needs a T_drain bound and a declared crash fallback, where the process exits and PG decides the outcome.
underclaim_risk: Without NC4 the original invariant is actively harmful for security counters, because failed attempts must be charged.

title: Cancel-sweep harness: enumerate every await point dynamically ('poll N times then drop', N=0..K) under DST, with 8 oracles and a named regression corpus
summary: ENUMERATION. Cancellation can only happen between polls, so the set of observable cancellation points for one execution equals the set of Pending returns of the top-level handler future. Wrapper CancelAt<N>(fut): poll fut and count Pending results; when the count reaches N, drop fut. Run under the existing DST shell (tokio current_thread, paused clock, turmoil net, from as.dst-harness-spec) for N = 0,1,2,... until a run completes before reaching N. That gives K_total = the number of distinct cancellation points on this path. To make awaits that return Ready immediately into cancellation points too, every sim I/O shim (DB fake/proxy, Redis fake, upstream, Wasm host calls) returns Pending once before each Ready ('interleave pending', as in futures-test). K_total then equals the number of I/O awaits on the path. Each yield records a site id (#[track_caller] location in the shim plus the tracing span stack). The CI coverage report asserts that every site seen in the uncancelled run was cancelled at least once. MODES per site: (m1) drop, (m2) JoinHandle::abort, (m3) the client sends h2 RST_STREAM (real hyper path), (m4) h1 FIN, (m5) tower timeout fires, (m6) graceful-shutdown deadline, (m7) Wasm epoch deadline trap at that hostcall, (m8) kill -9 of the process at the site (a crash oracle that must give the same durable state as m1). ORACLES after each run: O1 DB snapshot == pre-request snapshot (mod sequences) iff no CP; if CP was reached, == committed state AND the idempotency row is 'done' with a matching response (NC1/NC2). O2 Pool hygiene with pool size forced to 1: the next 3 requests from a DIFFERENT principal return their own results; pg_stat_activity has 0 'idle in transaction' rows; pg_prepared_statements, pg_cursors and the savepoint count are back to baseline; pg-pool-style orphan check (query_start IS NULL AND state='idle') == 0 (NC3). O3 Accounting: exactly one debit >= cost recorded, Redis TTL != -1 on every limiter key, and the cancellation itself is charged (NC4). O4 Authz stage cancelled => Deny observed; no request admitted without a recorded decision (NC5). O5 Outbox: no external effect was emitted for runs without CP; at most one effect per (tenant, key, idx) across retries (NC6). O6 Liveness: the next request completes within T_drain, and no task stays parked longer than T_drain on a lock or permit (NC8, futurelock). O7 Wasm: the Store was discarded, the next request on a fresh instance succeeds, no host panic (I5). O8 Retry with the same idempotency key after the cancel returns the committed result or re-executes; never a permanent 409 (in_flight lease TTL).
specifics: Budget: K_total per handler is expected to be under 50 (to be measured in the spike). PR gate: all handlers x all sites x {m1,m3,m5}, pool size 1, plus 200 random seeds. Nightly: all 8 modes x 20,000 seeds with random site choice. Regression corpus (named cases, each must FAIL against the vulnerable version and PASS against the fixed one): sqlx#4393 (cancel during begin; vulnerable 0.9.0, fixed f1e94ec); diesel_async#304 (MySQL stale result; vulnerable 0.9.2, fixed PR #305); tokio-postgres#1374 (statement leak count > 0 on 0.7.18); redis-py#2624 shape replayed against redis-rs multiplexed and pooled connections; Go CVE-2025-47907 shape against our DB adapter (parallel queries + cancel during row decode); Wasmtime CVE-2026-27195 and RUSTSEC-2026-0354 (drop call_async after a yield, and while queued; vulnerable 41.0.3/49.0.2); omicron#3140 shape (mutex-protected multi-step update cancelled); futurelock omicron#9259 shape. Oracle self-test (as.oracle-mutation): mutate the pool checkin predicate to 'always reusable'; O2 must fail within 100 seeds. Implementation: about 150 LOC for CancelAt plus the interleave shim; real Postgres in the sim is non-deterministic, so use a pgwire-level fake for PR runs and real PG 18 (container under 500 MB) for nightly, accepting nondeterminism there.
overclaim_risk: Dynamic enumeration covers only the executed path. Branches not taken in the seed's run go unswept, so pair it with branch-coverage-guided seeds.
underclaim_risk: Using a fake DB for PR runs could miss driver-level bugs (all the instances above ARE driver bugs), so the nightly real-PG run is mandatory, not optional.
